title: How does the @Lock annotation and LockModeType work in Spring Data JPA, and when should you choose pessimistic locking over optimistic?
shortTitle: @Lock annotation, LockModeType, and when to choose pessimistic over optimistic

s1_definition.profdef: The `@Lock` annotation on a Spring Data repository method declares a `LockModeType` for that query. `PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (exclusive), `PESSIMISTIC_READ` takes a shared read lock, `OPTIMISTIC` checks the version at commit, and `OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT` bumps the version even on read. Pessimistic is chosen over optimistic when contention on specific rows is high enough that retry churn under optimism outweighs the cost of serialized waiting.
s1_definition.analogy: The LockModeType is the kind of lock the clerk puts on Rajesh's account file. PESSIMISTIC_WRITE is a padlock only you hold — nobody else can read-for-update or write until you finish. PESSIMISTIC_READ is a "do not change" sign others can also read under but nobody can edit. OPTIMISTIC is just checking the tamper seal at the end. You reach for the padlock (pessimistic) when you know many people grab the same file at once and you would rather they queue than all fail and retry.
s1_definition.oneliner: @Lock sets the LockModeType per query — use PESSIMISTIC_WRITE for hot contended rows, optimistic everywhere else.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `@Lock` annotation on a Spring Data repository method declares a `LockModeType` for that query. `PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (exclusive), `PESSIMISTIC_READ` takes a shared read lock, `OPTIMISTIC` checks the version at commit, and `OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT` bumps the version even on read. Pessimistic is chosen over optimistic when contention on specific rows is high enough that retry churn under optimism outweighs the cost of serialized waiting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The LockModeType is the kind of lock the clerk puts on Rajesh's account file. PESSIMISTIC_WRITE is a padlock only you hold — nobody else can read-for-update or write until you finish. PESSIMISTIC_READ is a "do not change" sign others can also read under but nobody can edit. OPTIMISTIC is just checking the tamper seal at the end. You reach for the padlock (pessimistic) when you know many people grab the same file at once and you would rather they queue than all fail and retry.

**One line to remember:** @Lock sets the LockModeType per query — use PESSIMISTIC_WRITE for hot contended rows, optimistic everywhere else.

sections.s2_technical:
You annotate a repository method: `@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` above a `@Query` (or a derived query). When called inside a transaction, Hibernate adds the database's locking clause. On PostgreSQL that is `FOR UPDATE`; on others `FOR UPDATE` or vendor equivalents. For example, `findForUpdate("SAV2001")` acquires an exclusive lock so no other transaction can lock or modify that row until commit.

`PESSIMISTIC_READ` takes a shared lock: multiple readers can hold it, but writers block. Use it when you must guarantee the row does not change while you compute something, yet you allow other readers.

`PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` is the common choice for debit/credit on a hot row. It prevents both concurrent reads-for-update and writes, fully serializing updaters.

`OPTIMISTIC` forces a version check even for a read, ensuring the entity you read was not changed by commit time. `OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT` increments the version, useful to lock an aggregate root when a child collection changes so stale aggregate reads are rejected.

You can also pass locks programmatically: `entityManager.find(Account.class, id, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` or add a lock timeout via `@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "2000"))`.

Choosing pessimistic over optimistic: pick pessimistic when the same row is updated by many transactions concurrently (livelock risk under optimism), when the critical section is short so lock-hold time is tiny, or when the business cannot tolerate retries (e.g., sequential ledger numbering). Prefer optimistic when contention is low, when you want to avoid holding database locks and deadlocks, or when the operation is idempotent and retryable. Senior nuance: pessimistic locks escalate deadlock risk, so always lock rows in a consistent order and set a lock timeout.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India issues sequential cheque-book numbers from a single counter row. Two requests must never get the same number. Optimistic retries could interleave badly and the business cannot tolerate gaps or duplicates. This is exactly PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on the counter row — serialize issuance.

Problem 2 — A nightly interest job reads an account's balance and must be sure it does not change mid-calculation, while still allowing other read-only reports. This is PESSIMISTIC_READ — a shared lock blocking writers.

Problem 3 — We must avoid deadlocks when locking multiple accounts (transfer between two). This needs consistent lock ordering and a timeout.

We will build a SequenceService (pessimistic write) and show lock ordering in a TransferService.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/lock-mode-service-1.0.0.jar

# Issue a cheque number (pessimistic write on counter)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/cheques/next

# Transfer with consistent lock ordering
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfer?from=SAV2001&to=CUR3001&amount=50000"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: two concurrent cheque-number requests; one transfer SAV2001 to CUR3001.

Step 1 — Request A calls nextChequeNumber. findForUpdate issues SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the CHEQUE_NO row, acquiring an exclusive lock. value is 1000.

Step 2 — Request B calls nextChequeNumber concurrently. Its SELECT ... FOR UPDATE blocks because A holds the lock.

Step 3 — A increments to 1001, commits, releases the lock. A returns 1001.

Step 4 — B's lock is granted. It reads the now-current value 1001, increments to 1002, commits. B returns 1002. No duplicate, no gap — the exact guarantee pessimistic write gives.

Step 5 — For the transfer, the service sorts ids so it always locks CUR3001 and SAV2001 in the same order regardless of direction, preventing a deadlock when a reverse transfer runs concurrently. It debits SAV2001 and credits CUR3001, then commits, releasing both locks.

```
Hibernate: select ... from counters where name=? for update
INFO  Issued cheque number 1001        (A)
INFO  Issued cheque number 1002        (B, after A released)
Hibernate: select ... from accounts where id=? for update  (ordered)
INFO  Transferred 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Two cheque-number requests + one transfer
    │
    ├─ SEQUENCE (hot counter row)
    │    A: SELECT FOR UPDATE CHEQUE_NO → lock → 1000→1001 → commit
    │    B: SELECT FOR UPDATE → WAITS → granted → 1001→1002 → commit
    │    (unique, gap-free)
    │
    └─ TRANSFER (two rows)
         sort ids → lock first, then second (consistent order)
         debit/credit → commit → release both
         (no deadlock vs reverse transfer)
    ▼
  Counters and balances consistent
```

```
  │       SequenceService         │

  ── LockModeType choices ──
  PESSIMISTIC_WRITE → exclusive (debit/credit, sequence)
  PESSIMISTIC_READ  → shared (read-stable during compute)
  OPTIMISTIC        → version check at commit
  OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT → bump version on read (aggregate root)

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. nextChequeNumber() → findForUpdate("CHEQUE_NO") [lock]
  2.   counter.next() → 1001
  3. commit → lock released → B proceeds → 1002
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Lock annotation in Spring Data JPA lets me attach a LockModeType to a specific query so Hibernate adds the right database locking clause. PESSIMISTIC_WRITE issues a select-for-update that takes an exclusive lock, which is what I use for debit and credit on hot rows or for sequence generation. PESSIMISTIC_READ takes a shared lock so multiple readers can proceed but writers block, which fits a calculation that must see a stable value while still allowing reports. OPTIMISTIC forces a version check even on a read, and OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT bumps the version so I can lock an aggregate root when only a child changed.

I choose pessimistic over optimistic in three situations: when the same row is updated by many transactions at once so optimistic retries would churn or livelock, when the critical section is short enough that holding a lock briefly is cheaper than retrying, and when the business simply cannot tolerate retries, such as issuing sequential, gap-free cheque numbers where two callers must never receive the same value. Everywhere else I default to optimistic because it holds no database locks, scales better, and avoids deadlocks.

In our National Bank of India system the cheque-number counter is a single hot row, so I lock it with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE and every caller serializes cleanly, guaranteeing unique and gap-free numbers. For transfers between two accounts I lock both rows pessimistically but always in a consistent order by sorting the account ids first, which is the classic way to prevent a deadlock against a simultaneous reverse transfer. I also attach a lock timeout via query hints so a stuck transaction cannot block others indefinitely.

The senior point I emphasize is that pessimistic locking raises deadlock and throughput risks, so it is a deliberate choice, not a default. I always lock rows in a deterministic order, keep the locked section as short as possible, set an explicit lock timeout, and monitor lock-wait times and deadlock counts in the database. If those metrics stay healthy, pessimistic locking on genuinely hot rows is the right tool; if contention is low, I stay with optimistic locking and a bounded retry.
